Where are they now: Phumeza Tisile

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
We told Phumeza Tisile’s story in 2015, the XDRTB survivor who had gone deaf because of the medication she was given, which saved her life but left her completely deaf. She went on to have a double cochlear implant as a result of crowd funding driven by Dr Dalene von Delft a fellow MDR TB survivor. We were at Tygerberg hospital with her mother and friends who raised the funding when she heard for the 1st time.
30% of patients treated for MDR TB experience this side-effect but it’s a choice between life and death. It starts with the loss of high frequency hearing which is often unnoticed and because it’s a rapid-onset loss of hearing, most state patients like Phumeza aren’t warned or given regular audio tests, so they wake up one morning stone deaf.


Summary:
. The treatment of XDR and MRD TB in those days was extreme, patients were having to take 20 different tables a day and their chances of survival were touch and go. This story also is an opportunity to look at the improved treatment, but TB remains one of the biggest health issues and COVID has made the situation far worse.
We first met Phumeza as a bewildered, extremely thin 23 year old in her shack in Khayelitsha. Her tale of survival was gruelling as so many died around her. She herself was at deaths door several times. Dalene did a crowd funding campaign and Phumeza had a double cohlear implant which we filmed and were there the day her implants were turned on and she heard for the 1st time in a year. An experience which John recounted at the opening of the new Tygerberg hospital wing.
Today Phumeza is 31. She can hear well, she is able to use her cellphone and hear calls without additional devices, she is also able to hear in large auditoriums, both of which is not necessarily possible after an inplant. After our story she went on t get her degree in Social Sciences at UCT. She continues to work as a TB activists for the NGO TB Proof and speaks at global conferences campaigning for safer drugs. She is a researcher trained by Stellenbosch University and is currently working in clinics in Khayelitsha on destigmatising TB patients. Now that the wearing of masks is no longer compulsory TB patients are once again being shunned by their community and families making access and treatment extremely difficult.

Script:


BIG UPSOUND of crashing sea
Script: Wind, crashing waves, seabirds calling - sounds this 32-year-old doesn't take for granted
Breath
Script “We first met Phumeza Tisile as a bewildered 23 years old, living in Khayelitsha. She had survived 3 and a half years, of gruelling treatment for extensively drug resistant TB- a highly infectious airborne disease. TB has killed over a million South Africans. Phumeza remembers, that the side effects from the medication, felt worse than the illness itself. But it was an injectable drug that stole her hearing - the choice back then- was deaf or dead
Breath
Script When Phumeza was first admitted to Cape Town’s specialised TB hospital, she says no patients were being discharged, from what was known as the pre-XDR ward
Insert 1 Phumeza “.Each and every month there were patients coming out there were body bags coming out instead of people being discharged, so I thought me too I will go out the hospital gates in a body bag
Script: In 2014 there were no clear treatment regimes and doctors were trying any drug combination they could - explains Dr Jennifer Hughes, who ultimately saved Phumeza life
Insert 1 Jennifer 2.43 “I feel like I am feeling in the dark half the time we are trying various combinations, but people have side effects they can’t tolerate certain drugs you are not sure which one are you supposed to stop, you are trying to reassure patients but you just don’t know yourself
Breath
Script: Isolated and unable to lip read, she recorded her experience in a blogg and her story spread. A young doctor, called Dalene von Delft, herself a survivor of MDR-TB, reached out to her .Together they campaigned for better treatment regimes
Script: Phumeza's only hope of hearing was a double cochlear implant, - a device inserted into the eardrum which transmits electronic signals to an external receiver. And we were there when, in 2015, Phumeza had them fitted, and for the first time in years heard her mother's voice again. It was profoundly touching.
Insert 2 Mom “ Phumeza how are you?”
Phumeza “Right.
Mom “Hayibo Are you alright can you hear me”
Phumeza “Well”
Mom “I am so happy to hear you – how great is God?
Script: There wasn't a dry eye in the room and her humour was back
INSERT 2 4.53 Phumeza “I don’t sound like you, you sound like a cartoon from Spongebob
I sound like a cartoon from spongebob, and how do you sound laughing
Script: The first months were tough, but she has never looked back. She told her story across the globe - and thanks to activists like Phumeza drug regimes have improved dramatically over the last 8 years.
Breath
After all these years we wondered: whatever happened to Phumeza, and we decided to track her down
LINK “ I am so excited to meet this incredibly brave and tenacious young women who now is 32.
Phumeza: I remember you guys. There were all these cameras and stuff. It was a bit overwhelming for me because it was the first time I was hearing. Obviously the first time with the cochlear implant is not like normal hearing like it is now. People didn't sound like people.So it took about six months to a year to be able to hear, like I'm hearing now.

Script: Simple things we take for granted became possible - like a chat with mom

Phumeza: So now being able to pick up the phone without even thinking twice, hello and stuff like that - it's really, really nice. It is not something I take for granted. It is a gift

Script: The other gift was music - it was the biggest standout moment in those first few months- a live concert in New York was possibly more memorable than addressing the United Nations

Phumeza: when people ask how it felt when I got deaf, I mean, the night before I got deaf I actually had earphones and I was listening to music ….So having that back like that performance in New York, that was great. That was really, really great.
Script: TB had stolen too many years - she was desperate to get back to her studies. She graduated from UCT with a Bachelor of Science degree in 2020- without any special favours
Phumeza: The year before my audiologist sat me down, she said you need to register with the disability unit, let them know that you are deaf. I didn't
Masa You decide to go mainstream
Phumeza: I like the challenge, I am not sure why, but I don't like special treatment.
Script: We returned to Brooklyn chest TB hospital - a place haunted with memories of waking up deaf - to visit an old friend so pivotal in Phumeza’s survival from XDR-TB.
Jenny .Phumeza case is almost what made me an activist in TB you know, it made me really strongly feel like we have to do something about this, can people not see how it is affecting people's lives
Script: Dr Jennifer Hughes now works as a researcher with the Desmond Tutu TB Centre
Masa: What's the situation now?
Jenny: The TB regimen, is so much better, they are shorter, we have fewer drugs ,we have better drugs .So now things are much different and it really is an exciting time to be in the TB world.

Masa: And what about the injection that could leave patients deaf?

Jenny: No, that was one of the first ones to go and really in the global TB world, South Africa really led the way….

Script: MDR TB remains a public health crisis, and TB is the biggest killer in South Africa.

Masa: Phumeza what message would you have to somebody who's suffering from extreme resistant TB right now?
Phumeza: So I know the big X even though it is the worst case of TB, it is curable. CUT
Script: For the new season in her life - it’s is worth fighting for
